catalog_locator: Part II Language, ch. 2 Phonology, sec. 2.9 Tones (p. 93, last paragraph) and sec. 2.9.1 Contrastive Tones in Khezha (p. 94) of the archive.org scan dli.language.0277
catalog_quote: Khezha may be referred as a nonrestricted level tone language, because, pitch of syllable does not rise or fall at the time of production in this language. Even in the pattern of their combination, various tones can freely be assigned to any individual syllables without restricting the number of occurrence throughout the entire word. [...] In Khezha, the relative tone levels play a very important role in its grammatical system. They are used to contrast every individual lexical item. That is, every syllable in Khezha has a tone and there is always a one-to-one correlation between the number of syllables and the number of tones in every utterance. For instance, só 'repeat', so 'drink', still sò 'count', 'bribe'. The only difference between them is that, the first word ends in a high pitched syllable, the second ends in a medium pitched syllable, while the third ends in a low pitched syllable. They do not differ in length or intensity from other syllables, but their contrast is manifested solely by pitch. Presently I have identified three primary tones in this language. They are marked as, High tone (H) só 'repeat' / Mid tone (M) (unmarked) so 'drink' / Low tone (L) sò 'count', 'to bribe'. All the tones in this language occur on the vowels of the syllables.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khezha is described as a level-tone language with three lexical tones (high, mid, low) on every syllable, assigned freely to any syllable of the word; the grammar contains no statement of word stress or accent at all. The only remark bearing on stress is that tonally contrasting syllables differ neither in length nor in intensity, only in pitch. No stress position is stated; the language should be treated as tonal with no reported word stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. For tone: the e- noun prefix normally carries low tone (Kapfo 1989: 68); allotones (H ~ HM, L ~ LM) and tone sandhi rules under compounding are given in 2.9.2-2.9.3 (pp. 95-97).
new_statements.domain_note: Word/syllable level (lexical tone on every syllable of every utterance); examples are citation forms of monosyllabic and disyllabic words. Both Kapfo works describe the author's own Pfutsero (Letromi) village dialect; Kapfo 1989 p. 67 notes each Khezha village has its own dialect.
new_statements.identity_note: Both Kapfo sources describe the author's native Pfutsero/Letromi village dialect of Khezha (Kapfo 1989: 67 'Pfutsero dialect'; Kapfo 2005: 92 'my village dialect Letromi'), with village-level dialect variation noted. Glottolog khez1235 = Khezha Naga; Wikipedia now files the language as 'Kuzhami' (the autonym in Kapfo's 2007 dictionary title Kuzhale-Chahale). Glottolog 5.3's langdoc page for khez1235 appears to point at nekk1240, suggesting a recent reorganisation of the languoid; no separate dialect glottocode identified.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Khezha is described as a non-restricted level (register) tone language with three lexical tones (H, M unmarked, L) on every syllable; the grammar has no stress or accent section anywhere in the phonology chapter (sections 2.1-2.9 cover sounds, phonemes, contrasts, allophones, distribution, diphthongs, clusters, syllable, tones). The nearest thing to a stress statement is the remark that tonally contrasting syllables 'do not differ in length or intensity', i.e. pitch alone carries lexical contrast. The word 'stress' occurs only once in a linguistic sense, at p. 162 on the optional particle leh: 'In such a case, it stresses vowel so that the acoustic duration becomes longer. But this is only the case of intonation and not phonemic as such' - emphatic lengthening treated as intonation, not a phonemic word-stress rule.
new_statements.exceptions: none about stress; on tone, section 2.9.2ff. describes tone sandhi (the pitch of a following syllable is often affected by the preceding tone) and the potential particle lo whose mid tone becomes high after L or H (p. 162)
new_statements.identity_note: Kapfo describes his own variety; on p. 92 he names his village dialect Letromi and notes village-to-village dialect differences (in vocabulary, not stated for tone/stress). The book is catalogued by Glottolog as 2004 and printed as 2005 (CIIL); the archive.org item dli.language.0277 is a Digital Library of India scan with a text.

sources.note: No stress or accent section; the phonology chapter has no word for 'stress' at all. Sec. 2.9.1 (p. 94) says every syllable carries one of three level tones (H/M/L), that minimal sets 'do not differ in length or intensity from other syllables, but their contrast is manifested solely by pitch', and that Khezha is a 'nonrestricted level tone language' where tones are assigned freely to any syllable of the word (pp. 93-94). Sec. 2.8 (p. 91) says the language is open-syllabic and nouns are minimally disyllabic (e- prefix on monosyllabic roots).

sources.citation: Kapfo, Kedutso. 1989. Tones in Khezha noun constructions. Linguistics of the Tibeto-Burman Area 12(2): 67-78. DOI 10.15144/LTBA-12.2.67
sources.note: Nothing on stress/accent (a full-text search for stress/accent scanned for stress, accent, intensity, prominence, loud: no hits). States (p. 67-68) that Khezha is a tone language with three levels H/M/L; 'Tone is an obligatory feature of the syllable; every syllable occurs with a tone'; the e- prefix 'occurs simply to give greater phonological weight to the attached syllable' and normally carries low tone; describes tone alternations in noun compounding/derivation (Pfutsero dialect).

sources.note: The inventory lists 53 segments for Khezha: 8 vowels, 42 consonants and 3 tones, the tone segments being level ˥ (high), ˧ (mid) and ˩ (low) (values table: ˥ 'tone', ˧ 'tone', ˩ 'tone'); i.e. a three-level lexical tone inventory taken over from Kapfo 1992 via Ramaswami's compilation. Note PHOIBLE's RA contributor page says the Ramaswami data 'contain only phonemes, with no information on allophones or linguistic tone', yet the Khezha row of the same page shows Tones = 3.
